title: Rise before the hoary head (Leviticus 19:32)
hook: "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honor the face of the old man"
tomorrow: Saba needs knee surgery. so why is he also asking for prayers?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yehuda ben Tema's ages: counsel at fifty, gray hair at seventy, strength at eighty. Every age has its task. Today, what the rest of us owe those years.
screen: `EVERY AGE HAS ITS TASK.` → `WHAT WE OWE THOSE YEARS.`

segments.voice: A crowded bus. An old man climbs on, holding the rail, and suddenly every seated person finds their phone fascinating. Nobody saw him. Of course nobody saw him. Leviticus has a verse for that exact moment, and the strange thing is how it ends. "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and thou shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD." Why bring God into a seat on a bus?
screen: `EVERYONE FINDS THEIR PHONE.` → `RISE UP BEFORE THE HOARY HEAD.` → `WHY BRING GOD INTO IT?`

segments.voice: Rashi, reading the Talmud, solves it. Standing up is something only your own heart can check. A person might shut their eyes, as if they never saw the old man come in, and who could prove otherwise? So the verse adds: fear thy God. The one who knows whether you saw. That's the puzzle's first answer. There's a second oddity: the verse names two people, the hoary head, and the old man. The Talmud, in the tractate Kiddushin, argues over who counts. One view reads the old man as someone who has gained wisdom. Isi ben Yehuda says the hoary head means any elderly person at all, learned or not. Years alone are worth standing for. And the Talmud tells of Rabbi Yochanan, who would rise even for elderly Arameans, people outside his own community, and say: how many experiences have passed over these. Not their status. Not their faith. What their lives had carried. So an eighty-year-old standing for someone older isn't backwards. Every age owes honor to the ones further down the road. Something to tell a friend tonight: a sage in the Talmud stood up for elders of another people, because of everything their years had seen.
screen: `ONLY YOUR HEART CAN CHECK.` · `TWO PEOPLE IN ONE VERSE.` · `ANY ELDER, LEARNED OR NOT.` · `HOW MUCH HAS PASSED OVER THESE.` · then, large: `HONOR THE OLD.`

segments.voice: Stand up slowly, the way you would if someone you deeply respect had just walked into the room. While you're standing, name one elder in your life, close or not, and one thing their years have carried. Then sit, and keep them in mind for the rest of the sit.
screen: `STAND UP SLOWLY.` · `NAME ONE ELDER.` · `WHAT THEIR YEARS HAVE CARRIED.`

segments.voice: Rise before the hoary head: Leviticus's command to stand for the old, and to remember that God sees whether you noticed them.
screen: `RISE BEFORE THE HOARY HEAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: honor the old, for everything their long years have carried. See you tomorrow, then.
